Mary Queen of Scots. A Scottish monarch born in fifteen forty-two and executed in fifteen eighty-seven, the tragic focal point of religious and political turmoil in Renaissance Britain. Born Mary Stuart, she became queen of Scotland as an infant and married the future French king, inheriting a complex claim to the English throne through her descent from Henry the Eighth. Her Catholic faith, romantic entanglements, and rivalry with her Protestant cousin Elizabeth made her a symbol of religious conflict. Ultimately imprisoned in England for nineteen years, she was executed on charges of conspiracy, leaving behind a legendary legacy of ambition and persecution.

Become queen of Scotland at age six following her father's death at Solway Moss. At fifteen, she married the Dauphin of France, later Francis the Second, making her both Queen of Scotland and Queen of France by marriage.

She returned to Scotland as a widow in fifteen sixty-one, inheriting a nation divided by religious strife. Scotland was transitioning to Protestantism while Mary remained staunchly Catholic. Her marriage to Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley—grandson of Margaret Tudor, daughter of Henry the Eighth—produced James the Sixth of Scotland, who became James the First of England, uniting the Scottish and English royal lines.

Implicated in the murder of Darnley in fifteen sixty-seven, she was imprisoned and forced to abdicate. She fled to England seeking protection from her Protestant half-brother.

Elizabeth the First kept her imprisoned for nineteen years. Mary's Catholic supporters viewed her as the rightful English queen and a threat to Elizabeth's Protestant throne. In fifteen eighty-seven, after the Babington Plot—a Catholic conspiracy to assassinate Elizabeth—was uncovered and traced to Mary's private correspondence, she was executed, cementing the religious divisions that had haunted her reign.
